articles.title: Why this northern B.C. community is giving out 23-year-old toilets for free
articles.summary: The District of Port Edwards is giving away free low-flush toilets that have been sitting unused in the district office basement for the past two decades.

image.caption: Port Edward District staff members Alex Sirovyak and Chelsea Franco stand with Chief Administrative Officer Tyson Schofield as they prepare to hand out free toilets to residents. The toilets were originally part of a water conservation initiative the district ran in 2003. (Sumi Ragu/CBC)

blocks.text: British Columbia
The District of Port Edwards is giving away free low-flush toilets that have been sitting unused in the district office basement for the past two decades.
The low-flush toilets were part of Port Edward's water conservation initiative from 2003
The small community of Port Edward just south of Prince Rupert in northwest B.C. is giving out free toilets to its residents distributed on a first-come first serve basis.
The low-flush toilets have been sitting in Port Edward's district office basement for the past two decades, leftover stock from a previous water conservation initiative in 2003.
"They're taking up a lot of space down in our basement," explained Tyson Schofield, the district's chief administrative officer.
"I thought, 'This is not a good use of these toilets. Let's get them out for their intended purpose and let's get them out to the residents what they were used for.'"
Schofield started his position with Port Edward, which had 470 residents as of the 2021 census, in June after moving from the City of Delta.
When he discovered the 35 toilets collecting dust in the office basement, he decided to revive the program and give them away for free.

On Thursday Aug. 27, the district announced on social media it would be giving away free water-reduction toilets using an image of Oprah Winfrey and the words, "You get a toilet! You get a toilet! You get a toilet!"
By the next day, 18 toilets had already been claimed by residents.
Teresa Andrews is a Port Edward resident who came to the district office to pick up a free toilet for herself and her sons' houses.
"It's a great thing for them to do for us," she said. "It means that we're upgrading our toilet without having to go to the hardware store and buy one."

Schofield said he did some research into the original 2003 program, and found Port Edward had been reconstructing its water treatment plant at the time, and to get grant money for the project the community had to lower its water usage.
"From conversation with the community back then, it came up that we could install some low-flush toilets, so that's why they were purchased," he said.

items: More stories from Northern B.C.

blocks.text: Schofield emphasized that the toilets are over 20 years old, so he can't guarantee their quality.
But he said they recently installed two of them in the district office and they've been working well.
"They might not be the perfect toilet," he said. "However, it's always good to reduce the use of water. "
ABOUT THE AUTHOR
Hanna Petersen is a reporter for CBC News, working out of the Prince George, B.C., bureau. You can email her at hanna.petersen@cbc.ca.
Sumi Ragu

articles.title: Winnipeg's 1st female mayor wants to see a 2nd. That's not likely in this fall's election
articles.summary: Susan Thompson is the first — and only — woman to serve as Winnipeg's mayor. Nearly three decades after she left office, she says it's taking too long for a second woman to be sworn in.

image.caption: Susan Thompson remains the only woman to serve as Winnipeg's mayor more than 30 years after she was sworn in as the first in 1992. (Kevin Nepitabo/CBC)

blocks.text: Susan Thompson is the first woman to serve as Winnipeg's mayor. Nearly three decades after she left office, she says it's taking too long for a second to be sworn in.
"Our city is over 150 years old, and I'm still the only woman to have become mayor. We have to change that," said Thompson, who was the mayor of Manitoba's capital from 1992 until 1998.
But it doesn't appear that will change soon.
As of Saturday morning, none of the 11 people who had registered to run for mayor in the city's upcoming October election are women.
Thompson wants to see women sign up before the Sept. 22 registration deadline passes.
"It's been over 30 years since there's been a woman leader, and it is time," Thompson said.
She said her gender was often an issue for other people when she ran for office and led the city in the 1990s.
Many those issues persist today, Thompson said.
Four years ago, she told CBC News there needs to be "another seismic shift" in order to achieve gender parity at city hall.
Despite making up half of Winnipeg's population, women remain underrepresented on city council. Just 37 per cent of council seats are currently held by women.
Barriers are still excluding many women from entering — or even considering entering — the Canadian political sphere, said Kelly Saunders, a political science professor at Brandon University.
On average, women hold about one-third of elected positions across all levels of government in Canada, she said.

items: A sit down with Susan Thompson
Former Winnipeg mayor Susan Thompson still hoping to see 2nd woman in the job, but prof says obstacles remain

blocks.text: "We make up half the population in this country and in this province and in the city, so I would certainly like to see more representation of women," Saunders said.
But Saunders isn't surprised women aren't running to become Winnipeg's next mayor.
They may be choosing not to run due to the harassment, threats and personal attacks that politicians can face, both online and in person.
These attacks can be more vicious and sexist when women and other gender-diverse people run for office, Saunders said.
Last year, the Winnipeg constituency offices of Manitoba Families Minister Nahanni Fontaine and Housing Minister Bernadette Smith were targeted by vandalism and fires.

items: Manitoba MLA Nahanni Fontaine calls threatening letters she received 'grotesque' after man, 72, arrested
NDP cabinet ministers won't be pushed out of politics by 'attacks' at offices, MLA Nahanni Fontaine says

blocks.text: Smith said the incidents were an "attack on democracy" and Fontaine said the acts wouldn't scare the ministers out of politics.
Despite the hazards of working in politics, Saunders sees more and more young women filling the seats in her political science classes, she said.
'Blood sport'
"It's not that women aren't interested. It's … the fact that there are larger structural systemic barriers that make it that much harder for us to run and to be successful at running," she said.
"I think until we really address the larger problems in our political system … it's going to remain a pretty exclusive place, where a lot of people just don't feel welcome."
When Thompson first ran for public office in Winnipeg, she was warned that politics is a "blood sport."
But she worked to avoid hostility in order to focus on important issues and meeting municipal goals, she said.
She "wouldn't allow bad behaviour" while leading the city, she said.
"You want to see honesty, integrity, courage, leadership — and you want to see the job done. You don't want to see bad behaviour," Thompson said.
Waverley West Coun. Janice Lukes, a longtime fixture on Winnipeg city council, agreed that "politics is not for the faint of heart," in an interview on Up to Speed.
"It can get really nasty, but if you're dedicated and committed, you will succeed and move mountains," said Lukes, who was first elected in 2014.
Lukes decided not to run for re-election this year. In June, she told reporters that she felt she had accomplished what she set out to do when she entered municipal politics.
While she doesn't want to run for mayor, Lukes believes Winnipeg will eventually see another woman at the helm.

items: Waverley West Coun. Janice Lukes won't run for re-election
Outgoing Winnipeg councillors back candidates to succeed them as election registration opens

blocks.text: In Brandon, Manitoba's second-largest city, there are no women on the mayoral ballot either.
As of Saturday morning, only incumbent Jeff Fawcett and former Progressive Conservative MLA Len Isleifson were registered to run.
Tracy Baker works to encourage more women to run for municipal office in Brandon as one of the co-founders of Her Seat at the Table.
Ward 1 Coun. Heather Karrouze is currently the only woman on the western Manitoba city's council. That means women make up less than 10 per cent of the 11-person leadership team.
Baker said council needs more gender diversity so it can better represent Brandon's residents.

"We're just trying to have literally our seat at the table, because we think it's very important that there is, first of all, gender equality, but also the different ideas and community involvement that come from both men and women are important," she said.

Baker said more women have expressed interest in getting into local politics since the group started in 2023, but there's a lot more work ahead before women are equitably represented on Brandon's council.

Kathy Valentino, president of the Association of Manitoba Municipalities, is a city councillor in Thompson in northern Manitoba, where women make up 50 per cent of the eight-person council — led by Mayor Colleen Smook.
Valentino said anyone who is interested in making a difference in their local community should step up and register to run.
"A municipality is made up of many different people with different experiences and ideas, and that's good and that's healthy," she said. "We need all people of diverse ranges to step forward."
The Association of Manitoba Municipalities has a resource hub on its website with information for people who are interested in running in the Oct. 28 general municipal election.
Thompson has long kept an eye out for local women who would make good candidates — and she wants other Winnipeggers to do the same.

items: Susan Thompson opens up about time as Winnipeg mayor in new candid autobiography

blocks.text: "If you see somebody that would make a good candidate, you have to encourage them," the former mayor said.
"Winnipeg has wonderful women, but it really does take a village to encourage candidates.… Get in there and support and encourage women to take on the challenge."

articles.title: Iceland voters reject EU accession talks
articles.summary: A nationwide referendum failed to win enough support to restart negotiations on European Union membership, despite geopolitical tensions in the North Atlantic.

image.caption: Iceland is already closely linked to the EU as a member of the European Economic Area and the free-movement Schengen zoneImage: Leonhard Foeger/REUTERS

blocks.text: Icelandic voters have rejected a plan to restart accession talks with the European Union, final referendum results showed on Sunday.
The 'No' camp secured victory with 52.8% of the votes, while the 'Yes' camp garnered 47.2% support, the official count published by public broadcaster RUV showed.
The capital, Reykjavik, was the only area in the island nation of 400,000 people to support the referendum.
Some 270,000 Icelanders were eligible to vote. There was no information yet about voter turnout.
Iceland debates joining EU amid Trump's Greenland interest
Neck-and-neck vote after long debate
Iceland has spent the better part of two decades wrestling with the question of becoming the bloc's 28th member.
The Nordic country originally applied to join the EU in 2009 following the global financial crisis, which hit the country particularly hard.
Accession talks were suspended in 2013 after a euroskeptic government took office.

Iceland's current left-leaning government, elected in 2024, originally vowed to hold a vote next year but brought it forward because of rising geopolitical tension over Russia's war in Ukraine and Greenland.
Fishing industry pulled weight
However, the decision puts to bed concerns among many voters that joining the bloc would undermine Iceland's sovereignty, with fishing rights a major concern.
The fisheries sector has been fiercely opposed to joining the bloc, with 90% of industry players against the idea.
The result is a disappointment to Brussels, which had appeared willing to compromise on thorny issues, including fishing and farming, to facilitate Iceland's accession.

articles.title: Zambian opposition leader charged with treason
articles.summary: Mundubile had previously gone into hiding at a United Nations building in Zambia's capital.

blocks.text: Zambian opposition leader Brian Mundubile has been charged with treason, his lawyer has said amid heightened political tensions in the country.
Mundubile was arrested on Thursday, after a deadly raid by the authorities led the opposition politician to go into hiding.
He had disputed the results of the country's recent presidential election, which saw incumbent President Hakainde Hichilema securing a second term.
The authorities then accused Mundubile's NRPUP party of planning an armed insurgency, which it denied.

On Saturday night, Mundubile's lawyer Milner Katolo announced that his client had been charged with treason. The opposition leader looks forward to answering the accusation in court, Katolo told the Zambian Eye, external.
The lawyer said 17 others, including Mundubile's running mate Makebi Zulu, had also been charged with treason.
Mundubile gained 38% of the vote in the 13 August election, while Hichilema secured 60%, official results show.
The day after the poll, security forces raided a property in the capital, Lusaka, linked to Mundubile, killing a former cabinet minister and arresting a number of other politicians.
Following the raid, Mundubile and Zulu took refuge at a United Nations building in the city. The pair were detained after the president put pressure on the UN to hand them over.
The opposition was unable to mount a legal challenge to the election outcome as the courts were sealed off by the authorities on Monday, the final day that a case could be filed.
Hichilema is due to be sworn in for a second term on 1 September.

Regional and international observers described the election day as largely peaceful, but Zambia's Human Rights Commission has called for accountability over people whose whereabouts remain unknown following arrests and security operations around the elections.

articles.title: Greece, Turkey clash over protected Aegean marine areas
articles.summary: Turkey has announced the creation of two protected zones in a disputed area of the Aegean Sea, sparking an angry reaction from Greece. Does this mark a new chapter in a long-running dispute between…

image.caption: Turkey recently designated two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean, one off the Greek island of Lemnos (seen here in May 2025)Image: Diogenis Dimitrakopoulos/DW

blocks.text: A stint of unfamiliar calm between Greece and Turkey lasted less than three years.

After a devastating earthquake struck Turkey in February 2023 and Greece provided substantial aid, the two countries came closer together. They then signed the Athens Declaration on Friendly Relations and Good-Neighbourliness in December 2023, a further step to improved relations.

During this unusual time of calm, neither government moved to resolve long-lasting Greek-Turkish disputes, which mostly involve marking maritime boundaries. As a result, even a measure ostensibly aimed at protecting the environment has reignited regional tensions.

The latest dispute was triggered by Turkey's designation of two marine parks in the Aegean Sea and eastern Mediterranean earlier this month. The park in the northeastern Aegean includes a protected area in the waters between the Greek islands of Lemnos and Samothrace. The southern park lies east of Rhodes and surrounds the Greek island of Kastellorizo.
For decades, Greece and Turkey have been at odds over the delineation of their maritime borders in the Aegean and the related economic rights, such as claims to natural resources like oil.

Greece's Foreign Ministry was quick to react to the announcement, calling the establishment of the parks "illegal." In a statement, it said the designation of Turkish marine parks in areas outside Turkey's territorial waters has no legal validity.

Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis said at a Cabinet meeting earlier this week that he wanted to maintain good relations with neighboring countries. However, he stressed that "areas under Greek sovereignty are determined by international law" and that Greece is "always ready to defend them."
Competing to protect the Mediterranean?

For its part, Greece also announced two marine parks in 2025 — in the Ionian Islands and the southern Cyclades, both within Greek territorial waters. At the time, Turkey reacted in a clearly worded statement: "Unilateral actions should be avoided in closed or semi-closed seas such as the Aegean and the Mediterranean."

But Turkey has now declared its own marine parks — and without consulting Greece. Environmental protection appears to have been, at most, a secondary concern for the two countries in announcing their respective conservation parks. Instead, the move appears to be a new tactic for asserting dominance in the disputed maritime area — the latest chapter in a decades-long regional spat.
Kastellorizo caught up in Greece-Turkey dispute (09.2020)

Greece believes Turkey sees the marine parks as a way to challenge the sovereignty of Greek islands. It fears the designation of the two parks is part of Turkey's revisionist "Mavi Vatan" doctrine, Turkish for "Blue Homeland."

Under the doctrine, Turkey lays claim to the exclusive economic zones of Greece and Cyprus — maritime areas in which a coastal state has special rights, including over fishing and the exploitation of natural resources. It also challenges the sovereignty of numerous Greek islands and islets.

Until now, the doctrine has largely remained theoretical and strategic in nature. It is now being advanced through legislative initiatives in Turkey's parliament, and Turkey intends to use the parks to formalize its claims to greater control over parts of the Aegean and eastern Mediterranean.
Greece invests in defense

Greece itself is content with the status quo in the Aegean but feels threatened by Turkey, which is significantly better armed. As a result, Greece has invested heavily in fighter jets, frigates, submarines and air defense systems.

After spending significantly less on arms imports for several years, Greece ranked 19th worldwide among the largest importers of major arms from 2021 to 2025, according to the Stockholm International Peace Research Institute.

Even as Athens builds new or closer alliances, Turkey is factored into decisions. In 2021, for example, the Greek government sent Patriot air defense missiles to Saudi Arabia, despite objections from the Greek opposition, to protect Saudi oil refineries from Houthi attacks — at a time when Riyadh and Ankara were at odds politically.
During a state visit with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman, Prime Minister Mitsotakis explicitly referred to Turkey's "destabilizing and counterproductive" role.

blocks.caption: Greek Prime Minister Kyriakos Mitsotakis (right, seen here with Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman in Athens in July 2022), has worked to build closer ties with Saudi ArabiaImage: dDimtiris Papamitsos/Greek Prime Minister's Office/AP/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: Relations between Ankara and Riyadh have since improved. In early August, Turkey, Saudi Arabia and Pakistan signed the Mecca Defense Pact, a major joint defense agreement.
An 'Iron Dome' for Greece

With Turkey in mind, Greece has also pursued strategic cooperation with Israel. Despite heavy criticism in Greece over the dire humanitarian situation in Gaza, Mitsotakis continues to maintain close ties with Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu.

The Greek Defense Ministry is planning an air defense shield over the Aegean modeled on Israel's Iron Dome. The project, dubbed the "Achilles Shield," is designed to protect against all conceivable threats — including those from neighboring countries — and is expected to be fully operational by 2029.

For now, Mitsotakis continues to strike a conciliatory tone toward Turkey. But Greece is due to elect a new parliament by spring 2027 at the latest, and Mitsotakis may face growing pressure to take a tougher nationalist stance As the election approaches.

articles.title: India's citizen-led school audits test limits of activism
articles.summary: The student-led "Cockroach" movement is taking its campaign for accountability to government schools, but the activists' methods are encountering growing resistance from authorities.

image.caption: The CJP has said many government schools are in need of improvement Image: Madhan Kumar/DW

blocks.text: The Indian activist movement dubbing itself the "Cockroach Janta Party (CJP)" shot to national prominence in May by leading weeks-long protests over a scandal involving highly competitive entrance exams.
The student-led campaign put the government under intense political pressure and ended with the resignation of Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan in July.
Now, the CJP is taking aim at India's government schools, organizing volunteer visits to classrooms, documenting conditions and demanding accountability for problems.

Launched on August 15, Independence Day in India, the campaign asks parents, students and volunteers to inspect schools and record basic facilities including toilets, drinking water, electricity, classroom furniture and school buildings. The CJP has said the findings will be used to pressure authorities to make improvements.
The initial target is to audit 100 rural government schools over two months. It has also proposed giving recognition to village leaders who improve their schools.

Unlike the first campaign, which was based on street protests, the school audits require a more sustained form of local activism. Volunteers are expected to work consistently at the local level, document conditions and follow up with officials, parents and communities.

blocks.caption: Students celebrated in New Delhi after the resignation of India's education minister in JulyImage: Raj K Raj/Hindustan Times/Sipa USA/picture alliance

blocks.text: The organization is dealing with different layers of the Indian administration. Responsibility for government schools is divided between state governments, local administrations and elected village bodies. The CJP is therefore set to tackle different rules and political interests across the country.
India has over a million government schools, according to Education Ministry data. They make up nearly 70% of all schools in the country but serve less than half of its 247 million schoolchildren.
CJP: 'We are not afraid'
That scale has given CJP a vast field for its campaign. But it has also brought a new set of challenges.
The authorities are raising questions regarding rules and locations for the CJP scrutiny, as well as safeguards when children are present.
The response is already varying from state to state. Some authorities have ordered their own inspections, while others have restricted access or taken police action against CJP volunteers.
Authorities in Maharashtra and Rajasthan states have objected to school visits carried out without permission.
In one case, a complaint by school authorities resulted in police action against CJP members after they entered the premises to conduct an audit.

In Rajasthan, restrictions have been imposed on outsiders entering government schools, as well as on filming, interviews and other forms of documentation. CJP volunteers in Rajasthan have also said they were attacked while inspecting a school.
"We are not afraid. We are seeking accountability from the government," said CJP spokesperson Ashutosh Ranka.
Officials say schools are not open spaces

In the state of Uttar Pradesh, Chief Minister Yogi Adityanath has ordered officials to conduct on-the-spot checks of school facilities and directed police to register cases over what he called misleading videos about schools and colleges.
India's 'Cockroach' protesters claim online censorship
The CJP has said such measures undermine public scrutiny. Authorities have said schools are not open spaces for unauthorized inspections, particularly when children are present.
Vinita Gursahani Singh, managing trustee of We, The People campaign, which works on citizen empowerment, said the limits are set by law.

"Under the Right to Information Act, any citizen can inspect schools but you need to submit an application. And that makes sense as there has to be consideration for students and teaching," Singh told DW.
"All public scrutiny is legitimate. It is our job to scrutinize. But the scrutiny has to follow process. It has to be even-handed. What applies to one citizen must apply to all," she said.
Can activists serve as inspectors?
The CJP maintains government schools are publicly funded institutions and citizens have a legitimate right to ask how they are functioning.
Its volunteers use standardized audit forms to record conditions and send their findings to the CJP, which has said it will use the material to press local administrations to respond.

But critics question whether citizen activists can assume the role of inspectors. There are concerns about whether volunteers have the expertise to assess safety or infrastructure problems and how allegations posted on social media are verified.
Mohandas Pai, an education advocate, supports CJP's focus on government schools but disagrees with its methods.
"I like young people taking interest in school education. It's a broken system, and we need reforms," Pai told DW.
But he objected to large groups entering schools and questioning headmasters and children.
"You can't just barge into a school just because you think you are entitled to do it," Pai said, stressing that "children have to have a safe, secure environment."
India's elementary school helping students escape poverty
Pai said the CJP should instead send small teams with permission, collect systematic data, publish regular reports and use the evidence to pressure governments.
CJP spokesperson Saurav Das rejected the argument that the campaign should rely on conventional channels, saying such approaches have failed to bring meaningful change.
Responding to Pai on X, he challenged him to join the next school visit and show the volunteers how it should be done.
Questions of student privacy
The audit campaign has also raised questions about privacy, consent and disruption of teaching when volunteers enter schools, film inside classrooms or question students.
However, Kavita Srivastava, president of the People's Union for Civil Liberties (PUCL) Rajasthan, opposes restrictions on outsiders entering schools and taking photos and videos in her state.

"Activists were visiting government schools to document their condition and demand accountability. Protecting children's privacy should not be used to prevent legitimate public scrutiny of government schools," Srivastava told DW.
A new role for the CJP
Activist Amrita Johri said the CJP's first campaign tapped into a longstanding accountability gap in India's examination system, which cost millions of young people time and money.
"The demand for accountability had popular resonance because there was no real response from the government," Johri told DW.
She backed the school audit campaign, saying public scrutiny should be welcomed.

"Public audits are an integral part of citizens' right to information and should be welcomed as an opportunity to fix accountability," she said. Johri added that the CJP needs to train volunteers, document problems and follow up with authorities to make the campaign effective.

articles.title: Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings over decades-old, unofficial 'zone' system
articles.summary: A downtown Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings of a new movie after the film’s distributor unexpectedly withdrew access — citing a decades-old practice in Canada that limits which…

image.caption: The Carlton, near the intersection of Carlton and Yonge streets, cancelled screenings of the new film 'Tony' in August. (Kate McGillivray/CBC)

blocks.text: Toronto

A downtown Toronto cinema says it was forced to cancel screenings of a new movie after the film’s distributor unexpectedly withdrew access — citing a decades-old practice in Canada that limits which theatres can show movies first.
'Tony' screenings cancelled after distributor A24 withdrew the Carlton's access

The Carlton had already sold tickets for its first week of screenings of 'Tony,' a new movie by Canadian director Matt Johnson, when it got word that distributor A24 would no longer be providing the film.
"They ended up telling us that they were pulling the film because of a clearance issue," said Stefan Kern, director of operations for Imagine Cinemas, which owns the Carlton.

Clearance, Kern explained, "typically revolves around the fact that another theatre is playing it in a close proximity geographically and so [the distributor is] going to hold that film and not provide it to us."
Independent theatres have long complained about the unofficial 'zone system' in Canada, in which distributors give only one theatre in a given area access to a new release.

items: Why only 9 Canadian screens can show The Odyssey as Nolan intended

blocks.text: This is far from the first time this has happened, Kern added.
"This was the third film that we've had recently that was pulled from us," he said.
A decades old system that 'privileges Cineplex'

According to Sonya Yokota William, director of the Network of Independent Canadian Exhibitors, the zone system has its roots in the pre-digital era, when studios would produce limited film prints of a movie, leaving theatres to jockey for who would get access first.
Now, she said, "this practice has lingered, and you'll find that it predominantly privileges Cineplex."
In Canada, Cineplex takes in about 75 per cent of the country’s box office revenue, she said. Of the country’s approximately 2,700 movie screens, more than half belong to the cinema giant.
Yokota William says that Cineplex’s market concentration has "twisted the incentives" for distributors deciding which theatres to prioritize for new releases.
"In some ways it's like it only makes good business sense for you to keep your number one customer happy," she said.
Why does Canada lack competition in so many industries?

In 2024, her organization surveyed the independent cinemas that make up their membership, finding that more than half said they had to wait for a nearby Cineplex to have a complete run of a new release before they were given permission to play it.

As Vancouver’s Rio Theatre described it in a 2020 petition calling out the zone system, "this kind of underhanded business practice has made it very difficult for independently owned theatres to survive."
Cineplex says that film distributors hold the power

Cineplex, meanwhile, wouldn’t comment on the zone system in Canada or on the cancellation of the Carlton's 'Tony' screenings, writing to the CBC that "it is up to film distributors to decide where they play their films."
At present, the movie is playing at two Cineplex locations near the Carlton.
A24 did not respond to questions from the CBC about why it initially promised the Carlton access to ‘Tony’ — or what triggered its decision to pull the film.
Kern, too, did not name Cineplex in his interview or in a release put out by Imagine Cinemas about the 'Tony' cancellations.

Instead, the release encourages patrons to direct their comments to A24, film director Matt Johnson or to the Competition Bureau to "lodge a complaint about unfair business practices being used in theatrical distribution in Canada."

items: Canada's Competition Bureau sues Cineplex for allegedly advertising misleading ticket prices

blocks.text: The Competition Bureau would not confirm whether it's reviewing any complaints related to the zone system, and said it has never issued any guidance in relation to theatrical distribution in Canada.
Though she supports looping in the Competition Bureau, Yokota William also hopes that raising awareness about the existence of the practice will help bring it to an end.
"I would love for filmmakers, producers, funders and the government to start making noise about this, even if they can't or don't make legislation," she said.
ABOUT THE AUTHOR

Kate McGillivray is a writer and newsreader in Toronto. She's worked for the CBC in Montreal, Sherbrooke and St. John's, and she always wants to hear your feedback and story ideas. Get in touch here: kate.mcgillivray@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Manhunt underway after woman killed in Swiss rave shooting
articles.summary: The shooting happened outside a rave in the northern Swiss town of Aarau. Police said they were still searching for the perpetrator.

image.caption: Police have launched a manhunt for the perpetratorsImage: Michael Buholzer/KEYSTONE/dpa/picture alliance

blocks.text: A 22-year-old woman has died ​after a ​shooting ​at ‌a rave ​in Aarau, Switzerland, ​police said Sunday.
Five other people, aged between 24 and 27, were wounded in the incident, some of them seriously, the police added.
A "manhunt" for the "unknown perpetrator(s)" is underway, the police said in a statement on X, adding that the motive and the exact circumstances of the incident were still unclear.
A large contingent of the Aargau Cantonal Police has been deployed and a probe into the incident has begun, the police said.
Police in Freiburg, in neighboring Germany, were also taking part in the manhunt, the German news agency dpa reported.

blocks.caption: Police officers patrolling a street in downtown Aarau Image: Michael Buholzer/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

blocks.text: Meanwhile, the Cantonal police said a ‌major ​operation was ongoing and asked people to stay away from the area. They have also appealed to people to share any videos or images of the incident.
What else do we know about the shooting?
According to Swiss newspaper Blick, the shots were fired before 3:00 a.m. local time (0100 GMT) during the annual Aarauer Rave.
The newspaper quoted police spokeswoman Vanessa Rumpold as saying that the shooting occurred at the Schachen race course where the techno party was being held.
Aarau has about 22,300 residents and is located about 40 kilometers (25 miles) west of Zurich.

blocks.caption: Police blocked off streets near the horse racing track where the rave was taking placeImage: Michael Buholzer/KEYSTONE/picture alliance

articles.title: JV Ejercito: 'Secret funds' should go only to law enforcement, security agencies
articles.summary: Senate Finance Committee chairperson Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday that under the proposed 2027 national budget, confidential and intelligence funds should only be allocated to agencies tasked with…

blocks.text: Published August 30, 2026 4:17pm

Senate Finance Committee chairperson Senator JV Ejercito said Sunday that under the proposed 2027 national budget, confidential and intelligence funds should only be allocated to agencies tasked with law enforcement, intelligence, and national security.
“Confidential and intelligence funds should be limited to agencies whose mandate is law enforcement, intelligence, and national security,” Ejercito told Super Radyo dzBB.
““Confidential funds do not mean they are unaccountable. Just because they are classified as confidential does not mean they should no longer be subject to accountability,” he added.

Under Joint Circular No. 2015-01, confidential funds (CF) refer to lump-sum amounts allocated to national government agencies (NGAs) for “surveillance activities in civilian government agencies intended to support the agency’s mandate or operations.”

Meanwhile, intelligence funds (IF) refer to lump-sum amounts provided to NGAs for “intelligence information gathering activities of uniformed and military personnel, and Intelligence Practitioners that have a direct impact on national security.”
Lawmakers are now scrutinizing confidential and intelligence funds more closely amid the ongoing impeachment trial of Vice President Sara Duterte.
Duterte is currently facing an impeachment trial on allegations of culpable violation of the Constitution, betrayal of public trust, graft and corruption, and other high crimes.
Article 1 of the impeachment complaint accuses Duterte of committing impeachable offenses through the “systematic misappropriation and irregular liquidation” of confidential funds.
These include P500 million released to the Office of the Vice President and P112.5 million released to the Department of Education during her tenure as education secretary.
As the trial enters its seventh week, Ejercito said the public should wait for the impeachment court’s decision on whether the trial will return to an afternoon schedule.

The House prosecution team earlier said it favored starting Duterte’s impeachment trial at 3 p.m. onwards, while the Vice President’s defense team said it would comply with any schedule changes implemented by the impeachment court.
However, Senate impeachment court spokesperson Reginald Tongol said the public should focus more on the evidence presented in the impeachment trial rather than changes to its schedule.
“What the public should be talking more about is the evidence being presented and the legal theories of both sides,” Tongol said.— MCG, GMA News

articles.title: S. Korea: COVID-19 surges; masks, test kits return to shopping lists
articles.summary: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits. All three major…

blocks.text: SEOUL — As COVID-19 infections begin to climb in South Korea, pandemic-era shopping habits are making a comeback, with people once again reaching for masks and self-test kits.
All three major convenience store chains — 7-Eleven, GS25 and CU — have seen a sharp rise in sales of related products over the past month, according to news reports Friday.

Sales of COVID-19 self-test kits at 7-Eleven, for example, recorded a 62 percent on-month rise from Aug. 1-26, while those of masks, cold medicine and fever and pain relievers rose 17 percent, 15 percent and 14 percent, respectively, data showed.

blocks.caption: Masks sit on sale at a GS25 convenience store in Seoul. (Yonhap)

blocks.text: GS25 also reported a 30.3 percent increase in test kits and a 10.3 percent gain in cold medicine over the same period. Demand was particularly strong for masks for children and infants, with sales more than quadrupling from the previous month, up 341 percent, officials said.
CU saw a similar trend from Aug. 1-23, with sales of test kits and cold medicine up 45.7 percent and 12.2 percent, respectively, from the same period a month earlier.

“Since mid-August, we’ve been asking parents to send their children to day care with masks after a series of cold-like illnesses accompanied by high fevers among 1- and 2-year-olds,” Hwang Ji-mi, a teacher at a day care center in Dongjak-gu, Seoul, told The Korea Herald.
Industry sources say the recent uptick in COVID-19 infections is bringing back the shopping habits that became commonplace during the pandemic.
The country’s COVID-19 detection rate reached 9.1 percent for Aug. 9-15, roughly 2.8 times the 3.2 percent recorded three weeks earlier, according to the Korea Disease Control and Prevention Agency.
The number of patients hospitalized with COVID-19 at general hospitals also rose 2.4-fold over the same period.
Cases are also on the rise in China, with about 522,000 new COVID-19 cases reported in July, including 487 severe cases and one death, according to local media reports.

“With schools back in session, we expect demand for test kits, masks and cold medicine to remain strong for a while. The change of seasons is also likely to give sales a further boost,” a GS25 official said. /dl

articles.title: N. Korea names new defense minister amid modernization drive
articles.summary: North Korea has replaced its defense minister in a reshuffle of senior military leadership, state media reported Sunday, as the country accelerates its military modernization push and tightens…

blocks.text: North Korea has replaced its defense minister in a reshuffle of senior military leadership, state media reported Sunday, as the country accelerates its military modernization push and tightens discipline within the ranks.

Kim Song-gi, director of the General Political Bureau of the North’s Korean People’s Army, was appointed as the country’s new defense minister, replacing No Kwang-chol, according to the North’s Korean Central News Agency.
No was removed as defense minister and from the party’s central leadership and appointed first vice-director of the Munitions Industry Department of the ruling Workers’ Party of Korea.
The reshuffle was decided at the second meeting of the ninth WPK Central Military Commission held the previous day, which was guided by leader Kim Jong-un, the report said.

In the latest reshuffle, veteran military official Pak Jong-chon was appointed vice-chairman of the WPK Central Military Commission after being re-elected as a member of the party’s Central Committee and Politburo.

Pak returned to the forefront of the North’s military leadership after stepping down from the Politburo and party secretary posts and being dropped from the Central Military Commission’s vice chairmanship in February. His removal at the time sparked speculation that he was stepping back from the front lines due to his age.
The vice chairmanship is a key post overseeing the North’s military policies. Leader Kim Jong-un chairs the commission.
The meeting “discussed a series of structural reorganization plans for the improvement and development of the future overall defense affairs,” the KCNA said.

The newly appointed commanders would “firmly arm themselves with the party’s idea of building a strong army” and implement the party’s military policies with “boundless devotion and extraordinarily high activity,” the report said.

In a separate dispatch, KCNA reported that Kim met with scientists, researchers and officials from major defense research institutions and awarded them state commendations for their contributions to developing new combat weapon systems and improving their performance.

Calling them “the greatest patriots and heroes,” Kim highly appreciated “the recent exclusive innovative military sci-tech achievements … as a great revolution that opened up a sure prospect for radically improving the modernity of our army’s combat weapon systems.”
The leader expressed expectation that the science researchers “would bolster up the arms of the self-defensive power in a more overwhelming and stronger manner,” the report said. (Yonhap) /dl

articles.title: As Germany's far right gains ground, coded symbols are hiding in plain sight
articles.summary: As Germany’s far right gains political ground, researchers say some of its supporters are becoming more comfortable signalling their views in public — sometimes without displaying an explicitly…

image.caption: A man wears a Lonsdale T-shirt at a rally for the far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) party in Quedlinburg, Germany, on Aug. 23. The British boxing brand has long been popular with the country's far-right groups, despite publicly distancing itself from the movement and fundraising for anti-hate

blocks.text: World

As Germany’s far right gains political ground, researchers say some of its supporters are becoming more comfortable signalling their views in public — sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol at all.
Supporters have co-opted everyday brands to signal their beliefs while skirting the law

As Germany's far right gains political ground in some parts of the country, researchers say some supporters are getting more comfortable showing their views in public — albeit sometimes without displaying an explicitly political symbol.
At recent rallies for the Alternative for Germany, or AfD, that coded language was visible on things as ordinary as a pair of sneakers or a T-shirt.

Researchers say logos for brands including New Balance and Lonsdale are increasingly used as dog whistles for nationalist and Nazi symbolism — something that is especially significant in Germany, where the display of Nazi symbols is restricted by law.

"What we noticed in the last couple of years is that frequently at these events, you see a lot of people who have different signs which relate to the extreme right," said Gideon Botsch, head of the Emil Julius Gumbel Research Unit on Antisemitism and Right-Wing Extremism at Potsdam University.
"Some are clear and open right-wing and neo-Nazi symbols ... others are opaque or playing the game a little bit."
Some have co-opted New Balance, taking the large "N" on the side of its sneakers to mean "nationalist" and "NB" for Nationale Bewegung, or "national movement," Botsch said.

Likewise, Lonsdale has seen renewed use of its sportswear by the far right in part because, he says, when worn a certain way the logo spells out NSDA — the abbreviation for Germany's National Socialist Party.
"Those who know will know; those who don't know will think this is harmless," Botsch said.

The ambiguity is significant because Germany's law against Nazi symbols "expressly covers flags, badges, uniform items, slogans and forms of greeting,” said Sophie Scheuble, digital policy and counter-extremism manager at the Institute for Strategic Dialogue.
So "most of what is worn at far-right events is therefore lawful, and this distinction is well understood within right-wing extremist scenes.”
Those restrictions have led to an increase in the use of symbols recognizable only to those who know what they mean, without crossing legal lines.

When the eastern German state of Saxony-Anhalt's domestic intelligence service updated its handbook on far-right symbols in May, Scheuble said, its director noted that most extremists avoid prosecutable symbols and instead rely on codes and catchwords.
What has changed, researchers say, is the political environment where those styles are appearing.
Changing political climate

The Alternative for Germany, or AfD, has grown from a fringe party in 2013 into the likely winner of an upcoming state election in Saxony-Anhalt. The party has been legally designated a far-right extremist group in the state.
If it wins, it would mark the first time a far-right party has had an absolute state majority in Germany since the Second World War.
Fabian Wichmann, an expert at the EU Knowledge Hub on Preventing Radicalization, said there is a growing "grey zone" between Germany's hardcore neo-Nazi movement and the broader populist right.
Members of neo-Nazi groups attend AfD rallies and meetings and have encouraged their supporters to vote for the party, he says, seeing its success as a step toward their own political goals.

"The AfD has a widespread and diverse group of followers," Wichmann said. At its election events and marches, "you will see people who look very normal in their clothing," wearing things like New Balance and Lonsdale.

He said not everyone wearing those brands is a neo-Nazi, but there are "also a lot of neo-Nazis who wear this kind of stuff because they have some typical symbols, some typical narratives they share."
But the bigger change researchers say they're seeing isn't in the clothing itself. It's in the willingness to display those signals openly.
Wichmann says that shift matches the growing strength of Germany's far right and the AfD.
"They feel like ... the culture, the temperature of a society is changing. And now it's possible to wear something like this without getting into conflict,” he said.
"There's a feeling of, 'OK, we are on the winner's side right now,' and that's the reason why they are so openly wearing it."
Lonsdale's decades-long battle
New Balance has no affiliation with Germany's far-right movement. The company did not respond to requests for comment, but in the past has said it "does not tolerate bigotry or hate in any form."

Likewise, Lonsdale has spent decades fighting its appropriation by the far right with anti-racism initiatives since it became popular among German skinhead and neo-Nazi subcultures in the 1980s and '90s.
But the British boxing and sportswear company says the phenomenon is returning.

"We have noticed that since around summer 2024, the Lonsdale brand has once again been increasingly worn by far-right extremists,” spokesperson Ralf Elfering said. "This earlier misuse of the Lonsdale brand — and the fact that we are seeing it again today — is very frustrating.”
Elfering said the company stops supplying retailers when it discovers Lonsdale is being sold in a clearly extremist context.

items: Germany tested by new divisions 65 years after Berlin Wall erected
65 years after the Berlin Wall was built, Germany’s east-west scars help feed a rising far-right party

blocks.text: Other brands, however, carry considerably less ambiguity, according to experts.
Botsch points to Thor Steinar, a brand known for Nordic and runic imagery that has long been associated with Germany's far-right scene.
"Thor Steinar … maybe is a clearer sign than New Balance or Lonsdale that somebody is part of the scene," he said.

The company's original rune logo prompted police seizures after German authorities argued it resembled banned SS symbolism. Higher courts ruled in 2008 that displaying the logo was not punishable, according to Scheuble, and the company had by then introduced a replacement logo.

Lisa Mayor is a current Arthur F. Burns Fellow, working with Deutsche Welle in Berlin. Originally from Thunder Bay, she previously spent years as an investigative reporter for The Fifth Estate and The National. Her current role is as a network producer for CBC's Parliamentary Bureau. Her work has been recognized with a Michener Award, several Canadian Screen Awards and RTDNAs. You can reach her at lisa.mayor@cbc.ca.

articles.title: Making ice cream for friends is my way of spreading joy — and cultivating some for myself
articles.summary: Elizabeth Hunt never anticipated she would become an ice cream artist. But when she was given a hand-me-down kitchen gadget, she learned about the joy of experimenting on a budget and personalizing…

image.caption: Elizabeth Hunt never anticipated she would become an ice cream artist. But when she was given a hand-me-down kitchen gadget, she learned about the joy of experimenting on a budget and personalizing gifts. (Submitted by Elizabeth Hunt)

blocks.text: This First Person column is the experience of Elizabeth Hunt, who lives in Montreal. For more information about CBC's First Person stories, please see the FAQ.
As she packed up her kitchen, my friend Alisha pulled a bright red appliance from the highest kitchen cabinet and turned to me: “Do you want this?”
“What is it?” I asked.
“An ice cream machine,” she said. “I’ve had it for years and literally never used it. If anyone can do something with this machine, it’s you.”

Over the past decade, Alisha and I had forged a friendship over feeding each other’s kids and supporting each other’s struggles. Alisha was dubbed the “Almond Mom” by our combined crew of five kids for how she describes food by nutritional value, not tastiness. I got a reputation for having “the good snacks,” mostly because I make a mean chocolate chip cookie and a buttery Nutella crepe.

I wasn’t sure if my baking and cooking skills extended to frozen treats, but moving homes can be stressful. I was more than happy to check “Figure out what to do with the ice cream maker” off Alisha's list.
So I shrugged and said, "Sure," as Alisha thrust the ice cream churner in my hands.
For the first couple of weeks, the appliance just sat on my counter as I debated whether to put it in storage, pass it on to someone else or try my hand at something new.

In one of my regular chats with my Matante Rose-Marie, I told her about the ice cream maker. My 82-year-old aunt immediately launched into a story from the 1960s when her sister (my mother) had run an ice cream shop in Old Montreal for a few years and how her grandfather had been a beurrier (butter maker) in Saint-Jean-de-Matha, Que. My aunt seemed convinced that I was simply accepting my lineage in the dairy arts.

So after some Googling and YouTubing, I attempted my first batch of ice cream. Vanilla was the simplest recipe. Plus, I’ve always heard that vanilla is the standard by which to judge any ice cream shop. If you can’t get vanilla right, don’t even bother with other flavours.
My first batch of vanilla ice cream was a little thin and soupy but surprisingly delicious. I was ridiculously proud of myself and wanted everyone to taste it.

So I made more. I experimented with flavours, sweeteners, types of milk and how many crushed cookies a batch of vanilla ice cream can handle (about 23) to make “cookies 'n' cream.” I learned that the right temperature and correct churning time are essential to making creamy (not soupy) ice cream.

When Alisha’s birthday came around, I promised to make any flavour ice cream she wanted. She was delighted that I was putting her neglected appliance to use. She chose raspberry and dark chocolate. I used real raspberries and chopped up squares of the intense dark chocolate that she and I often share after a glass of red wine and a long conversation.
Folded into the ice cream was also a message for Alisha: I have created something delicious and filled with love (and nutrients) because you deserve some joy.
Nicole was next. We have the kind of friendship where one of us can call the other at 4 a.m. because of a bad dream — or any worry, really — and be met with compassion and support.

One day when my daughter was 10 she noticed that I was sad and asked, “Mama, do you need parenting?” When I worriedly assured her that it was not her job to parent me, she rolled her eyes and responded, “Obviously! I was gonna call Aunty Nicole.”
Nicole hesitantly asked for rum and raisin ice cream. “This was my favourite flavour as a kid,” she said, “but the lactose in dairy doesn’t agree with me”.
I left her house with a mason jar full of raisins soaking in dark rum and a promise to figure out an ice cream she could eat with joy.

items: I grew up sharing food and meals. But that isn't always the Canadian way

blocks.text: The ice cream, made with lactose-free cream, turned out creamy and smooth and the plumped-up raisins provided pockets of sweet booziness (even though they all sank to the bottom during freezing, because I hadn’t yet mastered the intricacies of timing and temperature).
And yet, Nicole declared it the best ice cream she'd ever had.
Motivated by Alisha and Nicole’s enthusiasm, I asked more friends to describe an ice cream flavour they’d like to savour.
I learned to bloom matcha to make a strawberry-matcha concoction for my daughter’s friend’s 14th birthday (kids these days are way more sophisticated than I was in 1989).

When one of my buddies asked for tiger tail, which is almost impossible to find in Quebec, I recreated a taste combination that I’d never tasted or even imagined could exist: orange and black licorice.

All of these flavours stretched my abilities and forced me to get creative about sourcing ingredients within my budget. Specials after Valentine’s Day and Easter made chocolate more affordable. A kind café owner agreed to sell me exactly three tablespoons of good-quality matcha when I balked at the price of a full package. Buying recyclable cardboard containers at a restaurant supply store proved more affordable and easier to manage than chasing down my Tupperwares loaned to friends all over Montreal.

Several batches and birthdays later, the unthinkable happened: my churner stopped churning. I stared at the little machine on my countertop. I turned it off and back on. It made a sad little noise and then stopped. For good.

After a few days of living with the burnt-out little Cuisinart on my kitchen counter, I packed it up, dumped it at the local recycling centre and informed my friends that my ice cream era had come to an end.
I was not prepared for the wave of sadness that hit me.
“This is ridiculous,” I thought to myself. “I’ve known real grief in my life. This is just a hobby.” And yet, this sadness was real.
Somewhere between a Greek tragedy and a ridiculous soap opera, I’ve had the kind of life that makes therapists wince and friends gulp down their glass of wine. And then ask for another.

However, like many other people laden with a heavy past, I’m sick of my own story and tired of my own trauma. I thought “healing work’ would be full of revelation and closure. Mostly, it’s been about repeatedly greeting old emotional reactions and worn-out fears like houseguests who’ve outstayed their welcome.

items: Dieting culture stole years of my life. Then, I unlocked the key to break free

blocks.text: Slowly, I’ve been stitching together a lighter life for myself: weekly potlucks with friends, complimenting strangers’ outfits when I walk by, growing avocados and pineapples plants from kitchen scraps, learning Gen Z slang (to my kids’ dismay) and experimenting with ice cream flavours.

Within two days of my little Cuisinart being sent to recycling, Nicole had scoured the second-hand online markets, found the same churner model in another colour and dropped it off at my apartment. She didn’t want praise or repayment.

If you ask Nicole, she’d say that she had a vested interest in not losing her supply of lactose-free rum and raisin. But she understood something that I’m just starting to articulate: It’s not about the ice cream.

It’s about creativity and the joy of gifting a bit of pleasure. It’s about the conversations with friends who share their memories, tastes and wild inventions. It’s about the thrill of taking on a challenge and the sense of accomplishment from creating something delicious that makes people smile.
We need more pleasure and kindness in this world. I want to share my hopes and talents and the gifts I have to contribute.
Thankfully, there are lots and lots of people who value real connection, generously offer help and support, know how to look for and find joy and make space for the deliciousness of life.
And for them I make ice cream.
